passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of the novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. Eighty participants (mean age 52 ± 8 years; 45% female) were randomly assigned to receive either Hypotensol (n=40) or matching placebo (n=40) once daily for 8 weeks. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) were measured at baseline and at week 8 using an automated cuff. Baseline SBP was 152.4 mmHg (SD 10.2) for the Hypotensol group and 150.1 mmHg for the placebo group. Table 1 presents the week 8 mean values and the mean reductions for each group. The Hypotensol group showed a mean SBP reduction of 12.4 mmHg (SD 4.7) and a DBP reduction of 8.1 mmHg (SD 3.9). The placebo group had a mean SBP reduction of 4.2 mmHg (SD 5.1) and a DBP reduction of 2.3 mmHg (SD 4.2). The differences between groups were statistically significant (p<0.01). The investigators concluded that Hypotensol effectively lowers both systolic and diastolic pressures compared to placebo.
stem: Which group experienced the larger mean reduction in systolic blood pressure?

options.C: Both groups experienced the same reduction

explanation: The Hypotensol group had a mean SBP reduction of 12.4 mmHg, whereas the placebo group’s reduction was only 4.2 mmHg, indicating a larger effect in the treatment group.
trap: Some may incorrectly assume the placebo group had a larger reduction because the baseline SBP was slightly lower.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for placebo effect in this study?
explanation: Correct: A) Random assignment balances groups, the matching placebo controls for the placebo response, and double-blinding keeps expectations of participants and investigators from biasing results. Why the others are wrong: B) In an open-label design everyone knows the treatment, so expectations are not controlled. C) A crossover changes the order of treatments but by itself does not control the placebo effect. D) An observational study has no assigned treatment or placebo.
trap: A crossover design might appear attractive, but it does not eliminate the placebo effect if not properly blinded.

stem: What is the percent reduction in systolic blood pressure for the Hypotensol group?
explanation: Correct: B) Percent reduction = 12.4/152.4 x 100 = 8.1%, using the baseline as denominator. Why the others are wrong: A) 8.9% divides by the week 8 SBP (140.0) instead of the baseline. C) 10.3% does not correspond to the correct calculation. D) 12.4 is the reduction in mmHg, not a percent.
trap: Using the week 8 SBP (140.0 mmHg) as the denominator, which overestimates the reduction as 8.9% (option A).

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: Hypotensol reduces systolic blood pressure more than placebo
options.B: Placebo reduces diastolic blood pressure more than Hypotensol
options.C: Both groups experienced reductions in blood pressure
options.D: Differences between groups are statistically significant

explanation: The data show the placebo group’s DBP reduction was only 2.3 mmHg, whereas Hypotensol’s was 8.1 mmHg, so the placebo did not reduce DBP more.
trap: Swapping the two diastolic reductions and crediting placebo with the larger fall, although placebo lowered DBP by 2.3 mmHg versus 8.1 mmHg for Hypotensol.

stem: What was the mean systolic BP reduction attributable to Hypotensol beyond the placebo response?
explanation: Correct: 12.4 − 4.2 = 8.2 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: A) 4.2 mmHg is only the placebo reduction. C) 12.4 mmHg is the unadjusted Hypotensol reduction. D) 16.6 mmHg adds the two reductions instead of subtracting.
trap: Reporting the within-group reduction of 12.4 mmHg as the drug effect without subtracting the placebo response.
